name: KY-008 laser transmitter module
description: 650 nm red laser transmitter module (about 5 mW, Class 3R/IIIa): a 6 mm laser diode head with an on-board current-limiting resistor. Drive the S pin high (5 V nominal; works dimmer at 3.3 V) and it emits a red dot; low switches it off. The signal pin supplies the laser current (under 40 mA). Sold as: Keyes / HW-493 KY-008 laser transmitter module from the 37-in-1 sensor kits, 3-pin header S, (middle, unlabelled), -.
eli5: A tiny laser pointer: set the pin high and a red dot appears, set it low and it goes off. Never shine it in anyone's eyes.

pins.name: S
pins.description: Signal: high = laser on, low = off. This pin also supplies the laser current (under 40 mA).

pins.name: MID
pins.description: Middle pin, unlabelled. VCC on some variants; leave it unconnected so S alone switches the laser (tying it to 5 V can keep the laser on permanently).

buildNotes: Wire S to a GPIO and - to GND; leave the unlabelled middle pin unconnected. The GPIO powers the laser through the on-board resistor.
Laser safety: about 5 mW at 650 nm (Class 3R / IIIa). Never look into the beam or point it at people, pets, mirrors or vehicles.

The laser can draw close to 40 mA at 5 V. At 3.3 V GPIO level it draws less and is dimmer. An ESP32 pin copes; on a Raspberry Pi Pico or Raspberry Pi (about 12-16 mA per pin) switch it with an NPN transistor (e.g. 2N2222, 1 kOhm base resistor) with S fed from 5 V.
Never feed the module more than 5 V and never bypass the on-board resistor: the diode dies instantly.
Some clone boards differ; if S and - alone give no beam, check the silkscreen and your board's middle-pin wiring.

example.code:
from machine import Pin
import time

laser = Pin({S}, Pin.OUT, value=0)  # S high = laser on
while True:
    laser.value(1)
    print('LASER ON')
    time.sleep(1)
    laser.value(0)
    print('LASER OFF')
    time.sleep(2)

test.title: The laser switches on, then off again
